steps.say: A digit drawn on a sphere. Turn the sphere, and a network trained on upright digits changes its mind.
The power spectrum gives the same answer at every angle. The wrong one.
The bispectrum reads a two every time.

scenes.headline: bispectrum: an invariant that keeps the shape
scenes.sub: Why the power spectrum forgets, and how a few products remember
scenes.say: I'm Phasor. Let's see what a shift does to a signal's Fourier coefficients, and which products of them it cannot touch.

scenes.title: Shift a signal, watch the phases

heads: A shift turns every harmonic's phase
The power spectrum keeps only lengths
A triple product cancels the turn
params.power: power spectrum: lengths only, never moves
params.triple: first times second times conjugate third

steps.say: Slide a periodic signal. Each Fourier coefficient turns by its own frequency times the shift. The first harmonic turns once, the second twice, the third three times.
steps.term: Shift: the cyclic group acting on a signal

steps.say: The power spectrum keeps each coefficient's length and drops its phase. So it never moves. That is why it is invariant.
It is also why it is lossy. This twin has the same three lengths and different phases. Same power spectrum, different signal.
Multiply the first and second coefficients by the conjugate of the third. Their turns cancel exactly, so the product holds still, and it still remembers how the harmonics line up.

scenes.title: Rebuilding the signal from n numbers

steps.say: The selective version keeps n products, not every pair. The first gives the mean coefficient.
The second gives the length of the first harmonic.
Its phase is the one thing no invariant can know, because it is the shift. Set it to zero.
Now each remaining product has exactly one unknown, the next coefficient. Walk up the spectrum.
The whole signal comes back, in one fixed pose. That is completeness, with a linear number of entries.
Why it matters. The full bispectrum of one 256 by 256 image is 17 GB.
The selective one is 0.5 MB, and the image is still determined up to a shift.
steps.caption: 17 GB full, 0.5 MB selective

steps.say: The library does this for seven group actions: rings, circles, image grids, polygons, cube rotations, the disk and the sphere. Each one is a module with no weights.
On the sphere, completeness is a conjecture. The evidence is reconstruction: from 380 numbers, a solver rebuilt every digit they tried, up to a rotation.
Rotated Spherical MNIST. The bispectrum plus an MLP gets 95.8 percent. The spherical CNN and the tensor-product network get 96.1.
At batch 16 on an H100, 0.257 milliseconds, against 1.02 and 93.7.
The power spectrum, just as invariant, stops at 77.7.

scenes.title: Rotated test on an RTX 3090, one seed
scenes.note: 284x faster than the tensor-product network, not 364x
scenes.say: I ran the authors' script on a 3090. 95.74 against 96.11, the power spectrum at 77.90, the planar CNN at 13.47. Same table, one seed.

items.text: The MLP behind it has 230K parameters
items.say: The layer has no weights. The MLP behind it has more parameters than the spherical CNN.

items.text: Less data favours the spherical CNN
items.say: With less data, the learned spherical CNN wins.
And on the sphere, selection only saves a factor of three. The speed comes from skipping learned tensor products.

scenes.text: Triple products cancel the symmetry and keep the phases. A linear subset of them is enough to rebuild the signal.

recap: Power spectrum: invariant, but drops phases
scenes.say: Invariant, complete, and small enough to use. See you next time.
